summary: Data Mover: Durable pipeline run scheduling
description:
As a pipeline owner, I want to schedule saved pipelines and inspect each occurrence so unattended transfers remain predictable, traceable and subject to manual-run safeguards.

Status: Proposed / not started
Owner roles: Product / Engineering / Operations
Design: docs/plans/pipeline-scheduling-research.md
Backlog: docs/stories/pipeline-scheduling-epic.md
Architecture: APScheduler 3.x recurrence adapter; PostgreSQL schedule and occurrence storage; atomic enqueue; existing pipeline execution runtime. Nine stories; estimates and task breakdown deferred.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Owners can manage and preview one-time, daily, selected-weekday, and weekly schedules with explicit timezone and missed-run/overlap behavior.
2. Schedule state survives restart, and eligible occurrences create one committed queued run through atomic PostgreSQL dispatch, with retry-safe occurrence identity and no reliance on a single Connect worker.
3. Scheduled and manual starts enforce shared admission and existing readiness, ownership, credential, content, provider and destination-reconciliation safeguards.
4. Dispatch remains independent of HTTP traffic and long transfers, participates in application shutdown/drain, and has tested database recovery and deployment-ownership controls.
5. Missed, expired, coalesced, overlapping and blocked occurrences have retained, owner-visible outcomes; dispatch success is distinguished from transfer success.
6. Schedule revision changes, pause/retirement races, run retention and migration/deactivation behavior have explicit, tested contracts.
7. The app exposes schedule/occurrence/run correlation and actionable dispatcher health without leaking credentials, provider bodies or data values.
8. Automated PostgreSQL concurrency/failure tests and documented Connect acceptance demonstrate the planned behavior; all nine stories have named evidence.
9. User/operator/security documentation and release instructions agree with the selected PS-1 policies and describe limits during complete Connect downtime.

summary: Define recurrence policies and preview upcoming runs
description:
As a pipeline owner, I want to choose a recurrence and see upcoming local run times so I can understand when my pipeline will run before enabling it.

Scope: Introduce a recurrence adapter using a tested stable APScheduler 3.x release and explicit application policies for late, repeated, and nonexistent local times.
Depends on: None
Owner roles: Product / Engineering
Status: Proposed / not started
Verification evidence: Focused recurrence/policy tests cover month-end, leap day, year boundaries, DST gaps/folds, once-only completion, and agreement between preview and generated occurrences.
Backlog: docs/stories/pipeline-scheduling-epic.md#ps-1
acceptance_criteria:
1. Once, daily, selected weekdays, and weekly schedules accept a validated IANA timezone; invalid dates, zones, and recurrence fields receive field-specific feedback.
2. A server-side preview shows at least five upcoming recurring occurrences, or the single one-time occurrence, with timezone and UTC offset; dispatch uses the same recurrence adapter as preview.
3. Daily wall-clock schedules stay at the selected local time across 23-hour and 25-hour days; weekday names avoid APScheduler 3.x numeric weekday ambiguity.
4. Document and resolve the proposed DST policy before implementation: skip nonexistent local times and use only the earlier instant for a repeated local time. Preview, cursor advancement, and dispatch must agree.
5. Confirm the initial lateness, catch-up, overlap, edit/resume, and definition-snapshot contracts in the epic's policy table; make the chosen policies typed and independently testable.
6. Select and lock a tested stable 3.x dependency and update pyproject.toml, requirements.txt, and uv.lock consistently; the implementation must not depend on 4.x APIs or a shared persistent APScheduler 3.x job store.

summary: Persist schedules and occurrence identity across restarts
description:
As a pipeline owner, I want my schedules and their history to survive app restarts so that downtime does not erase when a run was due or what happened to it.

Scope: Add Alembic migrations and application persistence for owner-scoped schedules, revisions, occurrence records, and pipeline-run provenance.
Depends on: PS-1
Owner roles: Engineering
Status: Proposed / not started
Verification evidence: Migration and persistence tests demonstrate round trips, unique-key enforcement, provenance, run retention, retirement, and upgrade with pre-existing manual runs.
Backlog: docs/stories/pipeline-scheduling-epic.md#ps-2
acceptance_criteria:
1. Schedule records persist pipeline/owner identity, validated recurrence data, timezone, enabled state, revision, next due UTC instant, policy settings, and audit timestamps.
2. Occurrence records persist intended UTC time, schedule revision, dispatch outcome and reason, dispatch timestamp, and optional run reference; a database unique constraint enforces schedule ID plus intended UTC time.
3. Stable idempotency tokens fit the existing run-token limit and identify the same occurrence across retries, workers, and restarts.
4. Deleting or expiring an ordinary run does not erase occurrence identity or permit that occurrence to be dispatched again; retention rules preserve required reconciliation and deduplication evidence.
5. Existing manual runs remain valid without schedule provenance. Pipeline/schedule retirement retains necessary occurrence evidence and uses explicit foreign-key behavior.
6. Upgrade and rollback/deactivation procedures account for existing active runs and application compatibility; PostgreSQL migrations are rehearsed and local SQLite development/test behavior is defined.

summary: Atomically enqueue each scheduled occurrence once
description:
As a pipeline owner, I want a due occurrence to create one traceable queued run even when requests race or a dispatcher restarts.

Scope: Introduce caller-owned enqueue transactions and a PostgreSQL dispatcher that coordinates workers with row locks and occurrence uniqueness.
Depends on: PS-2
Owner roles: Engineering
Status: Proposed / not started
Verification evidence: Real PostgreSQL, separate-session tests inject failures around commit and race multiple dispatchers; each eligible occurrence has at most one committed queued run and no lost due state.
Backlog: docs/stories/pipeline-scheduling-epic.md#ps-3
acceptance_criteria:
1. Extract a transaction-aware enqueue operation that does not commit internally; preserve existing manual-run behavior through a compatible transaction owner or wrapper.
2. Within one database transaction, dispatch inserts the occurrence, creates its eligible queued run with an immutable current-definition snapshot, and advances the schedule cursor.
3. Due schedule selection uses bounded batches and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED with enabled/revision/due-time rechecks, consistent database time, and a documented lock order.
4. Concurrent dispatchers and repeated delivery of the same occurrence resolve to the existing occurrence/run without creating additional queue or audit events.
5. A crash before commit leaves the due occurrence recoverable; a crash after commit but before worker notification leaves a queued run discoverable by normal runtime polling.
6. A lost commit acknowledgement is resolved by the stable occurrence key after reconnecting; no path advances a schedule separately from persisting its dispatch outcome.
7. Database locks are not held during provider network calls or transfer execution, and successful-dispatch logs are emitted only after commit.

summary: Handle missed runs and overlapping transfers predictably
description:
As a pipeline owner, I want explicit behavior when the app was offline or my pipeline is still running so that scheduling does not create an unexpected backlog or competing transfers.

Scope: Implement persisted late/skip/coalesce outcomes and database-enforced per-pipeline admission across scheduled and manual start paths.
Depends on: PS-1, PS-3
Owner roles: Product / Engineering
Status: Proposed / not started
Verification evidence: Policy and real PostgreSQL concurrency tests cover multiple missed times, lateness boundaries, long outages, deferred/nonterminal runs, manual-versus-scheduled races, and bounded catch-up.
Backlog: docs/stories/pipeline-scheduling-epic.md#ps-4
acceptance_criteria:
1. On recovery, the proposed default dispatches only the latest missed occurrence within the configured lateness window, initially one hour; older or expired times receive auditable coalesced/skipped outcomes.
2. Catch-up enumeration and transaction sizes are bounded. Long outages and dense recurrences use recorded skipped ranges/counts with clear coverage instead of unbounded occurrence creation.
3. A scheduled occurrence is skipped with a visible overlap reason when the same pipeline already has a queued or nonterminal run, including a deferred compute-start run.
4. The pipeline admission lock is shared by manual and scheduled starts; concurrent starts cannot bypass the overlap rule, while repeated submission of the same valid intent resolves idempotently.
5. Busy-pipeline occurrences advance according to policy without silently becoming automatic retries or accumulating a hidden backlog.
6. Per-pipeline admission is not presented as protection for different pipelines or external writers sharing a target; existing provider fences remain authoritative and supported target conflicts have tested blocking behavior.
7. One-time schedules complete or expire visibly after their sole occurrence and are not recreated on restart.

summary: Apply current ownership, readiness, and transfer safeguards
description:
As a pipeline owner, I want scheduled runs to use my current access and the same safeguards as manual runs so that unattended execution cannot bypass a required check.

Scope: Extract request-independent readiness behavior and reuse existing credentials, pipeline policy, content guardrails, and destination reconciliation checks.
Depends on: PS-3, PS-4
Owner roles: Engineering / Security
Status: Proposed / not started
Verification evidence: Cross-layer tests compare manual and scheduled safety behavior, exercise revocation/credential changes and readiness failures, and verify zero destination writes when admission or pre-write checks fail.
Backlog: docs/stories/pipeline-scheduling-epic.md#ps-5
acceptance_criteria:
1. Dispatch and execution validate current ownership and active account state; disabled/deleted owners or inaccessible pipelines produce a persisted safe outcome and cannot trigger provider writes.
2. Scheduled runs resolve the owner's current encrypted credentials without requiring an active browser session, copied bearer/session tokens, or a fabricated HTTP request.
3. Remote readiness checks currently embedded in the manual HTTP route are available through shared application/worker behavior before destination changes, outside the dispatch transaction.
4. Scheduled execution retains route/writer policy, source availability, column actions, full-source content scans, provider compute-start authorization, and destination publication controls.
5. Credential, definition, and schedule revision changes are rechecked at their relevant boundaries; a run records the exact definition snapshot admitted for that occurrence.
6. Unresolved or uncertain prior destination writes remain blocked pending existing reconciliation; scheduler catch-up cannot create an automatic retry around that block.
7. Unavailable CSV uploads, unsupported routes, expired credentials, sensitive-data blocks, and provider readiness failures produce safe linked outcomes without exposing secrets or row values.

summary: Dispatch without browser traffic or long-transfer delays
description:
As a deployment operator, I want scheduling to remain responsive during idle hours and long transfers so that due work is discovered reliably while the app is running.

Scope: Integrate a separate bounded dispatcher task with FastAPI startup, runtime ownership, shutdown/drain, database recovery, and deployment ownership.
Depends on: PS-3, PS-5
Owner roles: Engineering / Operations
Status: Proposed / not started
Verification evidence: Lifecycle tests cover failed startup, cancellation, drain, long transfers, multiple dispatchers, database loss/recovery, and disabled/draft deployments without requiring HTTP traffic.
Backlog: docs/stories/pipeline-scheduling-epic.md#ps-6
acceptance_criteria:
1. A dedicated dispatcher starts only after the application runtime is ready and polls persisted due state at a bounded configurable interval, initially five seconds.
2. The dispatch tick does not wait behind a full transfer in the existing supervisor loop; provider work and blocking database operations do not block the ASGI event loop.
3. Dispatcher database work participates in runtime admission and drain. Shutdown stops new dispatch work and waits for admitted transactions before engine disposal.
4. Database outages leave schedules due, expose degraded dispatcher health, and retry with bounded backoff; recovery processes due work through the same lateness policy.
5. Multiple Connect workers or nodes can contend safely through PostgreSQL without sharing an APScheduler 3.x persistent job store.
6. Drafts, staging content, and deployments sharing the production database have an explicit dispatch-disable or deployment-ownership configuration, documented and tested before enabling dispatch.
7. Dispatch is opt-in for the owning deployment and defaults off until explicitly enabled there; the existing midnight probe remains independent. Documentation explains Min processes=1, startup, total-downtime limits, and scheduling latency.

summary: Create, edit, pause, and retire schedules in the app
description:
As a pipeline owner, I want to manage schedules next to my saved pipeline so that I can automate runs and understand the effect of every change.

Scope: Add owner-scoped schedule services, endpoints, and Hedron/HTMX controls with preview, optimistic concurrency, lifecycle actions, and mounted-path support.
Depends on: PS-1, PS-2, PS-4, PS-5, PS-6
Owner roles: Engineering / Product
Status: Proposed / not started
Verification evidence: Service/API tests cover owner isolation, CSRF, revision races, pause-versus-dispatch, edit/resume semantics and retirement; UI checks cover previews, mounted routes, keyboard flows, and form fallbacks.
Backlog: docs/stories/pipeline-scheduling-epic.md#ps-7
acceptance_criteria:
1. Owners can create and list schedules for an eligible saved pipeline, preview upcoming times, and explicitly enable dispatch with clear timezone, catch-up, and overlap copy.
2. Create/edit/enable operations validate server-side permissions and recurrence; one-time schedules require a future time at creation, and recurring enablement begins with the next future occurrence.
3. Editing a recurrence or resuming recalculates the next future occurrence; due times bypassed by the action have explicit audited disposition. Changes use an expected revision and stale edits are rejected safely.
4. Pause prevents future dispatch once it wins the schedule lock; a run already committed by dispatch continues unless cancelled through the existing run action. The UI explains this boundary.
5. Retirement removes future dispatch eligibility without deleting required occurrence, run, or reconciliation evidence. Pipeline deletion/deactivation has defined schedule behavior.
6. Every state-changing route enforces ownership, CSRF, and allowed methods, and supports root, Connect, and Workbench mounts with ordinary form/navigation fallbacks.
7. Keyboard operation, field errors, focus retention, narrow layouts, and polling do not lose unsaved schedule edits or silently enable a schedule.

summary: Show schedule outcomes, run links, and dispatcher health
description:
As a pipeline owner and operator, I want to distinguish due, dispatched, skipped, blocked, and completed work so I can tell whether scheduling and transfer execution are functioning.

Scope: Expose occurrence history and operational diagnostics with safe correlation, linked run outcomes, and schedule/dispatcher health.
Depends on: PS-2, PS-3, PS-6
Owner roles: Engineering / Product / Operations
Status: Proposed / not started
Verification evidence: Presentation, authorization, audit/log schema, redaction, pagination, retention and health tests use synthetic data; example history demonstrates each occurrence outcome and linked transfer state.
Backlog: docs/stories/pipeline-scheduling-epic.md#ps-8
acceptance_criteria:
1. Schedule views show next intended run, timezone/offset, enabled state, recent occurrence outcomes, intended versus actual dispatch time, and a link to any created pipeline run.
2. Dispatch outcome and pipeline outcome remain separate: queued is never displayed as transfer success, and blocked/skipped/coalesced outcomes include a safe actionable reason.
3. Create/edit/enable/pause/resume/retire actions are audited with actor and schedule revision; dispatch records schedule, occurrence, and run correlation without impersonating a browser request.
4. Add allowlisted diagnostic events and measurements for dispatcher heartbeat, lag, due backlog, dispatch failures, and skipped/blocked counts; health distinguishes disabled dispatch from failed dispatch.
5. Occurrence/history access is owner-scoped and paginated, with safe retained-record behavior after linked runs are deleted; logs and UI exclude credentials, raw provider bodies, and source cell values.
6. The operator runbook explains lookup by schedule/occurrence/run ID, recovery after database failures, and how to identify a missed or delayed dispatch without treating the midnight probe as proof of pipeline completion.

summary: Verify restart recovery and release on Posit Connect
description:
As a deployment operator, I want migration and failure scenarios demonstrated on Connect so that scheduled pipelines can be enabled with clear evidence and recovery instructions.

Scope: Run cross-layer acceptance, rehearse deployment/migration and disablement, record evidence, and update user/operator documentation.
Depends on: PS-4, PS-5, PS-6, PS-7, PS-8
Owner roles: Engineering / Quality / Operations
Status: Proposed / not started
Verification evidence: A release acceptance ledger records automated results, synthetic screenshots, Connect content/process configuration, deployment version, expected/actual UTC and local times, failure-injection outcomes, and remaining external checks.
Backlog: docs/stories/pipeline-scheduling-epic.md#ps-9
acceptance_criteria:
1. Acceptance demonstrates unattended pipeline dispatch and execution with closed app tabs and no keepalive traffic on a Min processes=1 Connect deployment using non-sensitive test data.
2. Restart before a due time, downtime spanning several times, crash before/after dispatch commit, database interruption, and recovery after committed enqueue all produce the documented outcomes.
3. Separate-process PostgreSQL tests demonstrate duplicate prevention and overlap admission; deployment acceptance covers competing dispatchers or an overlapping redeployment and draft ownership.
4. Demonstrate schedule edits, pause/resume, owner disablement, credential replacement, long-running transfers, blocked guardrails, and uncertain destination reconciliation without bypasses or leaked data.
5. Migration/deactivation/rollback guidance prevents old and new application versions from dispatching incompatible state and preserves already committed runs and occurrence evidence; re-enabling dispatch has a rehearsed procedure.
6. Record appropriate lint, format, types, migration, unit/integration, UI/Hedron, documentation and security checks with named evidence; skipped, licensed, or live-provider checks remain explicitly identified.
7. The release documents the selected policy defaults, dispatch latency, retention, permissions, deployment ownership and complete-Connect-outage limitations. All earlier story acceptance has implementation/evidence links.
